en: Mayon volcano has a six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone to keep people safe from sudden, deadly explosive eruptions.
Coastal towns near the Philippine Trench must evacuate to high ground immediately after a strong earthquake to avoid tsunamis.
The Pasig River in Manila is heavily polluted, so children should avoid touching its water to prevent skin diseases.
Baguio City in the Cordillera region has a cooler climate, helping visitors avoid heat exhaustion during the hot summer months.
The wet climate of the Sierra Madre mountains creates many mosquito breeding sites, so children must clear stagnant water to prevent dengue.
The Angat Dam in Bulacan supplies drinking water to Metro Manila, so protecting its surrounding forests prevents severe water shortages.
During an eruption of Taal Volcano, wearing N95 masks protects children's lungs from inhaling harmful and abrasive volcanic ash.
The strong underwater currents of the San Juanico Strait between Leyte and Samar can sweep swimmers away, making it dangerous.
Touching sharp coral reefs in the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park can cause painful cuts and infections, so snorkelers must only look.
Mount Pulag in Benguet has freezing temperatures at its peak, so hikers must bring thick jackets to avoid life-threatening hypothermia.
The Cagayan River is the longest in the Philippines, so communities along its banks must evacuate early during heavy monsoon rains to avoid floods.
The island of Camiguin has more volcanoes than municipalities, so residents must always keep emergency go-bags ready for sudden volcanic eruptions.
